newsitem.title: UK: Sinn Fein plan new talks with British officials.
newsitem.headline: Sinn Fein plan new talks with British officials.

text.p: The IRA's Sinn Fein political arm will hold talks on Wednesday with British officials to try to breathe new life into Northern Ireland's peace process, political sources said on Tuesday.

The talks, the second in a week since Britain relaxed a ban on contacts with Sinn Fein, come on the eve of a Dublin meeting between Britain's new Northern Ireland Secretary Mo Mowlam and Irish Foreign Minister Dick Spring.

The two sides said after their first meeting in 16 months last Wednesday that it was too soon to say whether they had improved prospects for an early Irish Republican Army ceasefire. But Sinn Fein said a start had been made on dealing with problems.

The British province has been tense for months following an IRA resurgence and violence by pro-British Loyalist groups. Many people fear that summer Protestant parades could spark serious street riots.
Mowlam, appointed after Labour won a May 1 election, is due to meet heads of Protestant groups whose annual parades inflame sectarian tension, according to Irish Roman Catholics.
The IRA has rejected international pleas to end a 28-year war aimed at ending British rule and uniting Northern Ireland with neighbouring Ireland.
But a lull in IRA hostilities has helped to create a climate for Britain to end an embargo on officials' talks with Sinn Fein while still ruling out ministerial meetings.

Britain and Ireland hope talks involving most Northern Ireland parties will rekindle the peace drive. The talks, chaired by former U.S.senator George Mitchell, have been riven with inter-party wrangling. Adjourned in March, they are due to restart in Belfast on June 3.
Irish republicans say the IRA will not call a fresh truce until Britain guarantees that Sinn Fein will get a place at the talks. Sinn Fein is barred because of IRA violence.

On Thursday politicians from most Northern Ireland parties - including Sinn Fein and the politicial wings of banned pro-British "Loyalist" guerrillas - fly to South Africa to see how fractured communities there work to resolve their problems.
But pro-British "Unionist" parties are adamant they will have no have truck with Sinn Fein during a three-day conference in South Africa.
Peter Robinson, of the Democratic Unionist Party (DUP) which refuses to talk to Sinn Fein said the South African event would not be used as a cover for Northern Ireland peace negotiations.

"There are no talks or negotiations in relation to Northern Ireland. It is entirely one-to-one meetings with South Africans dealing with negotiating skills that they received over the period 1990-94 in their negotations," Robinson told Reuters.
Sinn Fein's senior strategist Martin McGuinness will head the party's team in South Africa. Robinson said the organisers had met DUP demands to be "hermetically sealed" from Sinn Fein.

According to The Irish Times, the event is being convened by the John W McCormack Institute of Public Affairs of the University of Massachusetts in cooperation with South Africa's Department of Provincial Affairs and Constitutional Development.
